content: Nature may have fewer backup plans than we thought, leaving our food supply and climate more exposed when species disappear. The largest global study of its kind suggests that losing species can steadily erode the benefits ecosystems provide, including pollination, clean water, carbon storage, and natural pest control. Led by King’s College London and Imperial College London , the research challenges the assumption that many species are interchangeable and that a few losses make little difference. Working with the Natural History Museum and the Alan Turing Institute, the researchers combined 423 published studies and 222,829 data points from land, freshwater, marine, and estuarine ecosystems. Published in Nature Ecology & Evolution , their analysis produced a database more than twice the size of the largest previous effort. Across 23 categories of ecosystem services and functions, most benefits kept increasing as biodiversity rose. They generally did not level off once a small collection of species was present, suggesting that ecosystems have less spare capacity than scientists previously assumed. The findings call into question the extent of “functional redundancy,” the idea that different species can perform similar jobs and compensate when one disappears. If that backup were widespread, additional species would eventually contribute little to a particular service. Instead, the study found that greater diversity usually continued to bring benefits. Dr. Emma Moffett, the study’s lead author and a geography lecturer at King’s College London, said, “Our findings challenge the comfortable assumption has been that ecosystems carry plenty of backup, so losing a species here and there doesn’t change much. Across most of the benefits ecosystems provide that we looked at, the data doesn’t support that. The ecological benefits keep climbing as diversity rises, which means it is falling as we lose species.” There were exceptions. Protection against coastal flooding, erosion, and similar hazards showed relatively little sensitivity to biodiversity overall. These functions often depend heavily on a few foundational species, such as shrubs whose roots stabilize sand dunes. Conservation needs to account for both overall biodiversity and the outsized contributions of certain species. Protecting a wide range of species helps sustain many ecosystem benefits, while safeguarding foundational species preserves functions that others may be unable to replace. The strongest relationship between biodiversity and any measured service involved marine carbon sequestration, the capture and storage of atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) in ocean waters and sediments. This suggests that species losses could have especially important consequences for the ocean’s contribution to climate protection. Marine life helps move carbon through the ocean, from phytoplankton near the surface to microbial food webs involved in transferring it into deeper water. The findings point to the importance of diverse communities for blue carbon sinks in the ocean and coastal environments, including mangroves and salt marshes. However, the striking ocean result came from only a small number of datasets. The researchers identify this shortage of evidence as an urgent research gap, so the finding warrants further investigation. Dr. Moffett said, “The ocean result stopped us in our tracks. Carbon capture at sea responded to biodiversity more strongly than anything else we measured, and yet it’s one of the least studied areas we found. If the world is counting on blue carbon to help with climate change, marine life can’t be an afterthought.” The team also explored how these benefits could change by connecting its database to biodiversity projections under the socioeconomic scenarios used by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. One focus was natural pest control on farmland, where predators and other enemies of crop pests provide a service farmers receive for free. The model predicts that this protection would weaken under development driven by fossil fuels compared with a pathway less dependent on them. Countries experiencing rapid population growth and lower levels of development would face the sharpest losses. Dr. Will Pearse, an associate professor in evolutionary ecology in Imperial College London’s Department of Life Sciences, said, “We’ve known that biodiversity supports humanity by providing us with food, clean water, clean air, and so many other ecosystem services. But what this model gives us is a precise, global picture: we can now predict the benefits biodiversity provides anywhere, making it even easier to recognize and take advantage of those benefits.” The database and forecasts for all 23 categories are publicly available to support policy and planning. Reference: “Biodiversity safeguards ecosystem services and functions worldwide” by Emma R. Moffett, Joel H. Gayford, Lexi Chen, Olivia F. Morris, Yuming Shi, Lucy Somekh, Nicole Stasik, Andy Purvis, Guy Woodward and William D. Pearse, 6 October 2026, Nature Ecology & Evolution . A dinosaur fossil that sat unnoticed in a museum collection for nearly a century has turned out to belong to a previously unknown predator with enormous curved claws. The animal, roughly the size of a large tiger, lived in what is now Britain about 120 million years ago. The discovery was made by a research team led by University College London (UCL) using a fossil originally found on the Isle of Wight. Described in the journal Royal Society Open Science , the dinosaur is the first known European member of a mysterious group of meat-eating dinosaurs called megaraptorans. These agile predators walked on two legs and were closely related to tyrannosaurs, including the famous Tyrannosaurus rex . However, their hunting strategy was very different. Rather than relying primarily on powerful jaws, megaraptorans had relatively narrow heads and used their muscular arms and large, curved claws to capture prey. Some eventually grew into enormous predators comparable in size to the largest tyrannosaurs. The newly identified species, however, was among the earliest and smallest known members of the group. It lived during the Early Cretaceous period, approximately 120 million years ago. Researchers named the dinosaur Invictibellatrix amberina . The genus name Invictibellatrix translates to “unconquered female warrior,” recognizing the group’s eventual rise to dominance as massive apex predators. Remarkably, the fossil consists of a fragment from the back of the dinosaur’s skull that entered the Natural History Museum’s collection in 1924. Despite its scientific importance, it remained largely overlooked until researchers examined it nearly 100 years later. Lead author Dr. Cassius Morrison (UCL Earth Sciences) explained what the animal may have looked like and how it hunted. “Based on what we know about its closest relatives, Invictibellatrix would have been three to four meters long and just over a meter and a half in height – about as tall as a human. It would likely have had feathers, and its claws might have been about 10cm to 20cm long. It would have eaten small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals – occupying a similar role in the food chain to the hyena today. “It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex. We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight. They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small. “It is a real mystery that this fossil was overlooked for so long, sitting in a drawer for nearly 100 years. Lots of bones are found on the Isle of Wight – who knows what else is waiting to be discovered.” Although humans did not exist when these dinosaurs lived, Morrison’s comparison illustrates how the smaller predator’s size and hunting behavior might have made it particularly dangerous to human-sized prey. Megaraptorans remain among the least understood groups of large carnivorous dinosaurs, largely because their fossils are so rare. For years, scientists have struggled to piece together where they originated and how they spread across the ancient continents. One leading theory suggests that megaraptorans first evolved in Asia before traveling through Europe and eventually reaching Gondwana (including present-day Africa, South America and Antarctica). There, some species became apex predators, meaning they occupied the very top of their ecosystems’ food chains. Until this discovery, however, an important piece of evidence was missing. No megaraptoran fossils had ever been identified in Europe, leaving a major gap in the proposed migration route. The discovery of Invictibellatrix now provides direct evidence that these dinosaurs inhabited Europe. Co-author Charlie Scherer, a PhD student at UCL Earth Sciences, said: “This new species is the first proof we have that megaraptorans were also present in Europe and that they reached Gondwana this way rather than island-hopping further south.” To investigate the fossil, the researchers used computed tomography, or CT scanning, a technique that uses X-rays to examine the internal structure of an object without damaging it. The scans allowed the team to produce a detailed 3D reconstruction of the skull fragment, along with a digital model of the internal space that once housed the dinosaur’s brain. They then compared these structures with skulls and braincases from other carnivorous dinosaurs, including tyrannosaurs, spinosaurs, raptors, and various other predators that walked on two legs. Several unusual anatomical details helped distinguish the specimen from previously identified species. Among them were an oval opening where the spinal cord connected to the brain and a distinctive crest shaped like an hourglass. Together, these features convinced the researchers that the fossil represented a new dinosaur species. Computer algorithms provided further support. By comparing the fossil’s anatomical characteristics with those of other dinosaurs, the researchers repeatedly found that it belonged within the megaraptoran group. The researchers also investigated the evolutionary history of megaraptorans and how their geographic range changed over millions of years. Using mathematical models, they combined evidence from known fossils, evolutionary relationships between dinosaur species, ancient geography, and prehistoric climate conditions. Their results suggest that megaraptorans were distributed widely across the world during the Early Cretaceous (i.e., at the time of Invictibellatrix ). However, their fortunes appear to have changed dramatically over the following tens of millions of years. By the Late Cretaceous, the group had probably disappeared from Laurasia (including modern-day Europe), the vast northern landmass that once contained much of what is now North America, Europe, and Asia. Meanwhile, megaraptorans in the southern supercontinent of Gondwana became some of the most formidable predators of their time. Several evolved into enormous hunters equipped with curved claws reaching 35 cm (14 in) in length. One particularly impressive example was Maip macrothorax , discovered in what is now Argentina. Scientists estimate that this giant carnivore measured approximately nine to 10 meters long and weighed as much as an elephant. Exactly why megaraptorans disappeared from northern regions remains uncertain. The study did not establish a definitive cause, but changes in climate, shifting environmental conditions, and competition from other large predators, including tyrannosaurs, may have contributed to their decline. The fossil that revealed Invictibellatrix amberina was originally collected by amateur paleontologist Reginald Walter Tooley near the base of a cliff on the southwestern coast of the Isle of Wight. Tooley was an exceptionally productive fossil collector who discovered more than 1,000 specimens. Following his death, those fossils became part of the Natural History Museum’s collections. For nearly a century, the skull fragment remained among those historic specimens without its true identity being recognized. Professor Paul Barrett, the study’s senior author from the Natural History Museum, emphasized that even extensively explored fossil sites can continue to produce unexpected discoveries. “Despite over 200 years of collecting, the Isle of Wight continues to surprise us with new dinosaur species, and finds of carnivorous dinosaurs, such as Invictibellatrix, have been particularly elusive. “Work like this shows the exceptional value of working with historical museum collections where there are still many discoveries to be made.” The dinosaur’s name also carries a message beyond its evolutionary significance. In their paper, the researchers explained that Invictibellatrix was chosen to “give hope and strength to all those who are bullied, discriminated, victimized, and oppressed that tomorrow will be theirs and not to give up in face of such odds.” The species name amberina refers both to the amber preserved in the rocks where the fossil originated and to the female given name. The discovery highlights the continuing scientific importance of museum collections. Even specimens gathered generations ago can contain valuable clues about prehistoric life, and some may still represent species that scientists have never recognized. Reference: “A new megaraptoran dinosaur from the Lower Cretaceous Wessex Formation, UK, and its implications for theropod evolution and biogeography” by Cassius Morrison, Charlie R. Scherer, Philip Mannion, Laura B. Porro, Brett Clark, Daniel D. Folkes and Paul M. Barrett, 14 October 2026, Royal Society Open Science . DOI: 10.1098/rsos.260937 The research received funding from the Palaeontographical Society, the Royal Society, and UKRI. Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. Scientists may have found a surprising shortcut to nuclear fusion that could dramatically cut the energy needed to ignite the power of the Sun. Scientists at the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL) have identified a potentially much more efficient way to achieve nuclear fusion, the process that powers the Sun. Their calculations suggest that changing the order in which plasma is heated and compressed could dramatically reduce the energy needed to reach ignition, a crucial milestone in the pursuit of practical fusion power. For more than seven decades, scientists have relied on an equation called the Lawson criterion to determine whether plasma can remain sufficiently hot and dense for long enough to sustain fusion reactions without additional external heating. Developed in the 1950s, this equation establishes the conditions required for ignition, but it does not explain the most efficient way to achieve them. Now, PPPL physicists Luis Delgado-Aparicio, Masayuki Ono, and Jonathan Menard have updated that decades-old framework. By incorporating four additional factors that influence the behavior of fusion plasma, they have developed a more comprehensive model for determining how fusion systems should heat and maintain their fuel. Their findings were published in the journal Physical Review Letters . To understand the significance of the discovery, it helps to know what plasma is. Often called the fourth state of matter, plasma is a gas so hot that its particles become electrically charged. When plasma reaches ignition, the energy released by fusion reactions produces enough heat to sustain the process without further external heating. Achieving this condition efficiently is one of the central challenges facing fusion energy researchers. Delgado-Aparicio compares the team’s discovery to finding an easier route through a mountain range. Imagine that the energy required to ignite fusion is represented by a landscape, with the destination lying beyond a towering mountain. Many proposed fusion strategies take the equivalent of climbing directly over that mountain. They first increase the plasma’s density and then supply the heat needed to reach ignition. However, the researchers’ calculations point to a less demanding route: raise the plasma’s temperature first, then increase its density. “A lot of companies want to climb the mountain head-on and spend enormous energy to get there,” Delgado-Aparicio said. “Go around the peak instead. You reach the same place in a much smarter way, and you use far less energy.” The mathematical explanation involves a region called the Cordey saddle. Like a mountain pass, this represents the lowest point along a barrier separating plasma that still needs outside heating from plasma capable of sustaining its own fusion reactions. To evaluate possible routes, the researchers used a measurement known as Q, which compares the power generated by fusion with the external heating power supplied. In an ideal plasma containing only fusion fuel, the Cordey saddle occurs when fusion produces approximately five times the heating power being supplied. Conditions become more complicated in actual fusion machines. Contaminants within the plasma and extremely powerful magnetic fields can shift the location of this critical point, increasing the Q value needed to reach it. The findings could have important implications for the design of fusion machines called tokamaks and stellarators . Researchers and private companies are investigating several technologies that could eventually generate electricity for the power grid through nuclear fusion. Tokamaks are among the leading approaches. These doughnut-shaped devices use powerful magnetic fields to confine plasma while it is heated and brought to the density needed for fusion ignition. Identifying a more efficient path to ignition could help engineers make better decisions about how these machines are designed and operated. The work also supports PPPL’s broader efforts to address scientific and technological obstacles standing in the way of commercial fusion power and future fusion pilot plants. One major advantage of the new model is that it considers several important physical processes simultaneously. Previous studies often examined these effects separately, making it harder to understand how they interact under realistic operating conditions. The researchers incorporated four additional influences that can change the requirements for sustaining fusion: Considering these effects together produces a more realistic picture of the challenges that fusion reactors must overcome. “When you leave these effects out, you say the design will work fine,” Ono said. “When you put them in, the picture changes, and it becomes quite important.” According to Ono, the goal is to establish a common framework that scientists can use to evaluate proposed fusion systems before committing to construction. Treating the Lawson criterion as a single, unchanging threshold can overlook physical effects that substantially alter the conditions required for ignition. “Fusion experiments cost a great deal of money, and you do not want to make mistakes you could have caught beforehand,” he said. The analysis also highlights a potentially serious challenge involving the materials used to build fusion reactors. More than a dozen advanced fusion machines are being designed with tungsten lining their inner walls. Engineers favor this metal because it can tolerate the extraordinary heat associated with fusion plasmas, which must reach temperatures exceeding those at the center of the Sun. However, tungsten can create problems if even a small amount enters the plasma. The researchers found that a tungsten concentration of just one part in 10,000 could approximately double the pressure needed to achieve ignition. This means that an extremely small quantity of material released from the reactor walls could significantly increase the difficulty of sustaining fusion. Those calculations were based on a two-dimensional analysis. When the model is extended to three dimensions, the required pressure can rise beyond the limit at which the plasma remains stable. The results demonstrate why seemingly minor details in reactor design can have major consequences for fusion performance. Although energy losses make ignition harder, the researchers discovered that these same effects could also help prevent a different problem. Fusion scientists have long considered the possibility of thermal “runaway” instability. This occurs when heat from fusion reactions accelerates additional fusion, producing still more heat and potentially creating a self-reinforcing cycle. The new calculations indicate that the processes responsible for draining energy from plasma can also limit this feedback. Working together, these effects could allow a burning plasma to maintain a stable operating condition without continuous external heating. (Unlike a fission power plant, a fusion system holds only seconds of fuel at a time, so losing control means the plasma cools and the burn stops rather than anything worse.) This finding suggests that some physical processes traditionally viewed as obstacles to ignition may also contribute to the stability of a working fusion reactor. The research identifies potential ways to overcome some of the problems revealed by the new model. One promising option involves coating the inner walls of fusion systems with liquid lithium, a technology PPPL has investigated for years. Such coatings could reduce the amount of tungsten entering the plasma while also helping it retain heat. Another possibility is the use of spin-polarized fuel. This approach involves aligning the spins of fuel nuclei before fusion occurs, increasing the likelihood of fusion reactions and potentially improving the system’s performance. Together, these strategies could help engineers develop reactors that reach ignition more efficiently while maintaining stable conditions. For now, the proposed heat-first approach remains theoretical. The findings come from mathematical calculations rather than direct experimental measurements, since existing experiments have not reached the temperatures associated with the Cordey saddle. The researchers plan to investigate their proposed strategy further through computer-based experiments, which will allow them to test the heat-first route under simulated fusion conditions. “While more study is needed, we are excited by these results, and they suggest a clear path forward for future research in this area,” said Menard. The work offers a new perspective on one of fusion energy’s most persistent challenges. Rather than simply pushing plasma to ever-higher densities and temperatures, scientists may be able to reach the same critical destination by choosing a more efficient route. Reference: “Generalized Lawson-Cordey-Mills Accessibility of Fusion Ignition” by Luis F. Delgado-Aparicio, Masayuki Ono and Jonathan E. Menard, 10 September 2026, Physical Review Letters . DOI: 10.1103/mmc9-nzfx The research was supported by the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences, under contract DE-AC02-09CH11466.
